config.title: Build typed A B experiment assignment model

intro.title: Build typed A B experiment assignment model
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed A/B experiment assignment model in TypeScript. You will create a system that randomly assigns users to either a 'control' or 'treatment' group for testing different features. The core concept is using TypeScript's type system to define strict interfaces for experiments and assignments, ensuring type safety. You will work with interfaces, enums, and functions to implement the assignment logic. This will help you understand how to model real-world testing scenarios with robust, error-resistant code.
intro.usecase: A/B experiment assignment models are foundational to product optimization in tech companies like Netflix, Amazon, and Google. Developers use typed models to reliably assign users to different feature variations (like UI layouts, algorithms, or pricing displays) while tracking performance metrics. This pattern appears in dashboard configuration panels where teams define experiment parameters, target audiences, and success criteria. Implementing this with TypeScript ensures type safety across the entire experiment lifecycle—from assignment logic to data analysis—preventing runtime errors in critical business decisions.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript interface to define the structure of an A/B experiment.
Initialize a typed state object to hold experiment assignment data.
Implement a function to randomly assign a user to a variant (A or B).
Apply type guards to validate experiment assignments at runtime.
Configure a component to render content based on the assigned variant.
Integrate the assignment logic into a simulated user flow.
Manipulate the experiment state to toggle between variants for testing.

steps.title: Import TypeScript types and utilities
steps.instruction: Import the necessary TypeScript utilities and define the core types for the A/B experiment model. Start by importing the `useState` hook from 'react' and defining an interface for the experiment variant.
steps.hint: You'll need to import React and useState, then create an interface that describes what properties a variant should have.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react'
// Define an interface for ExperimentVariant with id (string) and name (string) properties
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have the necessary imports and a type definition ready for building the experiment model.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react', and an ExperimentVariant interface is defined with id: string and name: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've imported both React and useState, and defined the ExperimentVariant interface with the correct properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React and useState from 'react', then create an interface called ExperimentVariant with id and name properties.

steps.title: Define the ExperimentAssignment interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named ExperimentAssignment that defines the structure of an experiment assignment with proper type annotations.
steps.hint: Think about what properties an experiment assignment would need. You'll need to define the interface with the 'interface' keyword, a name, and type annotations for its properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a new interface named ExperimentAssignment that defines the structure for experiment assignments.
successCriteria: An interface named ExperimentAssignment is defined with proper type annotations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created an interface named ExperimentAssignment with the correct syntax and type annotations.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword followed by the name ExperimentAssignment and define its properties with type annotations.

steps.title: Define the ExperimentResult interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named ExperimentResult that has a property 'assignment' of type ExperimentAssignment and a property 'converted' of type boolean.
steps.hint: Define an interface with the name ExperimentResult, then add two properties inside it: assignment (type: ExperimentAssignment) and converted (type: boolean).
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named ExperimentResult with typed properties assignment (ExperimentAssignment) and converted (boolean) is added to the code.
successCriteria: The ExperimentResult interface is defined with the correct property names and types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check that the interface name is exactly 'ExperimentResult' and both properties (assignment: ExperimentAssignment, converted: boolean) are included.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ExperimentResult interface is not correctly defined. Ensure you create an interface with the specified properties and types.

steps.title: Create the assignToVariant function
steps.instruction: Write a function named assignToVariant that takes no parameters and returns either 'A' or 'B' randomly, with explicit type annotations for the return value.
steps.hint: Use Math.random() to generate a random number, then return 'A' if it's less than 0.5, otherwise return 'B'. Add type annotations for the function's return type.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named assignToVariant is defined with proper TypeScript type annotations that returns either 'A' or 'B' randomly.
successCriteria: The assignToVariant function exists, has explicit return type annotation, uses Math.random(), and returns either 'A' or 'B'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function has explicit return type annotations and correctly returns either 'A' or 'B' based on random chance.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Check that you've named it assignToVariant, added proper type annotations, and implemented the random assignment logic.

steps.title: Create the trackExperimentResult function
steps.instruction: Create a function named trackExperimentResult that takes an ExperimentResult parameter and returns void.
steps.hint: Define the function with proper TypeScript type annotation for the parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named trackExperimentResult that accepts an ExperimentResult and returns nothing (void).
successCriteria: The trackExperimentResult function is defined with the correct parameter type and return type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function accepts an ExperimentResult parameter and returns void.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or has incorrect type annotations. Check the parameter type and return type.

steps.title: Initialize sample experiment data
steps.instruction: Create two sample arrays using your interfaces: one for experiment variants and one for experiment results. Use the names 'sampleVariants' and 'sampleResults'.
steps.hint: Declare two const arrays with explicit types using your interfaces. For variants, include at least 'A' and 'B' variants. For results, include at least one result object with appropriate properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: Two typed arrays will be created: 'sampleVariants' containing variant objects and 'sampleResults' containing result objects, ready for use in later steps.
successCriteria: The arrays 'sampleVariants' and 'sampleResults' are declared with proper type annotations using your interfaces, containing at least one valid object each.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some sample data, but check that both arrays are properly typed and contain valid objects matching your interfaces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sample data arrays are missing or don't match the expected structure. Make sure to create both 'sampleVariants' and 'sampleResults' arrays with proper type annotations.

steps.title: Create the analyzeExperimentResults function
steps.instruction: Create a function named analyzeExperimentResults that takes an array of ExperimentResult objects as a parameter and returns an object with typed statistics.
steps.hint: Define the function with proper TypeScript typing for the parameter and return value. You can calculate statistics like total participants, conversion rates, or other metrics.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named analyzeExperimentResults is defined with proper TypeScript types for its parameter and return value.
successCriteria: The analyzeExperimentResults function is created with a parameter typed as ExperimentResult[] and returns an object with typed statistics.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but check that it has the correct parameter type (ExperimentResult[]) and returns a typed object with statistics.
steps.feedbackWrong: The analyzeExperimentResults function is missing or has incorrect TypeScript typing. Make sure to define it with proper parameter and return types.

steps.title: Create the main application function
steps.instruction: Create a function named runExperimentWorkflow that demonstrates the complete A/B experiment workflow using the functions and data you've already defined.
steps.hint: Inside the function, call assignToVariant, trackExperimentResult, and analyzeExperimentResults with your sample data, then return a string summarizing the results.
steps.expectedOutcome: A runExperimentWorkflow function that calls your typed A/B experiment functions and returns a summary string.
successCriteria: The runExperimentWorkflow function is defined, calls assignToVariant, trackExperimentResult, and analyzeExperimentResults, and returns a string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the function, but make sure it calls all three experiment functions (assignToVariant, trackExperimentResult, analyzeExperimentResults) and returns a string summary.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't properly demonstrate the complete workflow. Check that it uses the functions and data you've already defined.

steps.title: Execute the experiment workflow
steps.instruction: Call the main application function you created earlier and log its returned results to the console.
steps.hint: Use console.log() with the function call as its argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console will display the experiment analysis results when the code runs.
successCriteria: The main application function is called and its return value is logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling the main function and using console.log() with its return value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main function wasn't called or its results weren't logged. Check that you're using console.log() with the function call.

steps.title: Test type safety with intentional errors
steps.instruction: Add a function call that intentionally passes incorrect types to one of your experiment functions to see TypeScript's compile-time error checking.
steps.hint: Call assignToVariant with a number instead of a string for the userId, or call trackExperimentResult with mismatched property types.
steps.expectedOutcome: TypeScript will show compile-time errors when you intentionally pass wrong types to your typed functions.
successCriteria: An intentional type error is added that violates the expected parameter types of one of the experiment functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a function call, but it might not have a clear type error. Try passing a number where a string is expected, or vice versa.
steps.feedbackWrong: No intentional type error was added. Try calling assignToVariant with a number instead of string for userId, or trackExperimentResult with wrong property types.
